newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan reforms seen hurting weaker banks.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan reforms seen hurting weaker banks.

text.p: Pakistan's proposed reforms of the state financial sector are likely to make life difficult for small private banks, according to a research report by a local brokerage house.

"More stringent regulatory and capital requirements coupled with a harsh operating environment will force smaller and weaker capitalised banks in the private sector to increase capital," KASB & CO said in a report received by Reuters on Wednesday.

Shahid Javed Burki, economic advisor to the caretaker government, told reporters on Monday the monitoring powers of the State (central) Bank of Pakistan (SBP) would be enhanced as part of comprehensive reforms of the state-run financial sector.
Burki said the SBP would ensure effective supervision and enforcement of banking regulations and would strengthen them on capital adequacy and provisioning for loan losses and interest.
KASB & Co said in its report that the stricter regulations would require banks to conform to the internationally accepted capital standards of the Bank for International Settelments.
"We understand...the new standards will necessitate a risk adjusted capital adequacy, that is capital as percentage of risk weighted assets, of a minimum of eight percent," it said.
The report said most Pakistani banks calculate capital adequacy as a percentage of total demand and time liabilities, without factoring in risk weighted assets.

The risk adjusted capital adequacy ratio of most state-owned commercial banks averages around three percent, while most foreign and some new private banks are well above the eight percent level, the report said.
If the central bank chose to enforce the eight percent risk-adjusted capital adequacy requirement, growth for banks would become increasingly difficult without raising their capital base, it said.

Although most private banks are over-capitalised, more stringent measures would inevitably give the advantage to large capitalised foreign and some private banks, including Faysal Commercial Bank and Askari Bank, it said.
"We feel that the reforms will also expedite the consolidation period currently underway in the sector," the report said.
Burki said several state-owned financial institutions would be merged and restructured before being privatised.
KASB & Co said its sources in the central bank had indicated that amalgamation and takeover laws for the financial sector were being framed to speed up the process of weeding out the weak.

"In present conditions, our selection criteria for banks puts a much greater weightage on strong capitalisation and well managed institutions, which are capable of weathering the consolidation storm ahead," it said, recommending Askari Bank followed by Faysal Bank as their main picks.
